verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.1.7 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 1, the Sutikshna-Agastya frame). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. I v. 7.
attribution_note: Agastya to Sutikshna, as stated (the text marks 'agastir uvaca' before the verse).
translation_note: Accurate. The next verse (1.1.8) completes the thought: liberation comes from neither action alone nor knowledge alone, but from both.
context: The Yoga Vasishtha opens with a frame story: the Brahmin Sutikshna, unsure whether action or knowledge leads to liberation, asks the sage Agastya. Agastya answers with this image of two wings and then tells the story of Karunya, who stopped all ritual action because two scriptures seemed to point in opposite directions, until his father set him straight.
core_teaching: Freedom is not reached by knowledge alone or by action alone but by both working together, as a bird needs both wings to fly.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: As a bird reaches its goal only with both wings, the highest state needs knowledge and action together, though not at the same instant: action purifies the mind, knowledge removes ignorance, as a mirror needs both cleaning and light.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. I)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders the two wings as knowledge and acts, and the following verse as: neither acts nor knowledge alone produce emancipation. Agastya then introduces Karunya's story to illustrate it.

practical_reading: Teachers use this verse against two opposite traps: thinking without ever acting, and busyness without reflection. When stuck waiting for certainty, take the next small step and keep reflecting as you go.
misreadings: Not a claim that action and contemplation must happen at the same moment; the commentary explicitly denies that
Not a dismissal of either study or work as unnecessary
cautions: In Advaita reading, 'action' here means duty and ritual that purify the mind; a modern 'just do things' gloss is a simplification
speaks_to: feeling stuck between overthinking and doing
students and professionals who read a lot but don't act
people who keep busy but feel directionless
not_for: someone exhausted or burnt out who needs rest rather than a push to act
a reader in acute grief

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.10.9 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 10, titled 'Raghava's dejection'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. X v. 9.
attribution_note: Spoken by Rama's attendants to King Dasharatha, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'durmanāḥ' is literally 'ill-minded, low in spirit'; Mitra has 'dejected'.
context: Rama has returned from a pilgrimage across the land and has withdrawn: he neglects his daily duties, eats little, and sits apart. His worried attendants report this to the king. In the following verses they list his symptoms (he performs his rites only sometimes, refuses food, takes no pleasure in play), and in the next chapter Rama is brought before the court, where the king and the sages question him gently.

key_terms.sense: dejected, low in spirit, troubled in mind

core_teaching: The verse simply reports that Rama has changed since his journey. The book treats this withdrawal as the start of a real search for meaning that needs a wise listener.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. X)
commentaries.gist: The servants tell the king they themselves have wasted away with worry; Rama has been dejected since the pilgrimage, carries out his daily rites only half-heartedly, and has stopped eating and enjoying pastimes.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: The commentator gives no separate gloss on this narrative verse; the chapter's colophon titles it 'Raghava's dejection' (rāghava-viṣāda), placing it as the opening of Rama's dispassion.

practical_reading: Loss of interest after a big experience (travel, a loss, a milestone) can signal that old goals no longer fit. It deserves attention and a good conversation, not dismissal.
misreadings: Not a romanticisation of depression as a spiritual stage
Not a claim that withdrawal is always a sign of wisdom
cautions: Rama's symptoms (not eating, withdrawing, neglecting duties) overlap with clinical depression; a reading must not suggest that such symptoms need only spiritual reframing. Encourage talking to someone, including professionals.
speaks_to: feeling flat or changed after travel or a major life event
parents or friends worried about someone who has withdrawn
not_for: someone in a severe depressive episode if the reading implies it is 'just a phase of awakening'
research_note: No commentary gloss on this verse; second note is from the narrative itself.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.11.37 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 11, titled 'Consoling Raghava'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XI v. 37.
attribution_note: Vishvamitra to Rama, as stated. In this sarga the king speaks at vv. 29-31, Vasishtha at 32-33, and Vishvamitra from v. 34 to 37.
translation_note: Fair. 'ādhayaḥ' are mental afflictions or anxieties rather than sorrows in general; the commentary links the promise to his gaining what he desires. 'You will have it' renders 'prāpsyasi'.
context: Rama has been brought before the court, pale and silent. The king and Vasishtha speak to him; then Vishvamitra asks why his eyes are so restless and what is troubling him, noting that the usual causes of distress don't apply to a prince like him. This verse is his closing invitation; Rama, encouraged, sheds his gloom and begins his long account of what troubles him.

key_terms.sense: whatever you have in mind, whatever you wish

core_teaching: A respected teacher invites the troubled young man to say openly what is on his mind, promising that speaking it out is the way to be freed of the anxieties.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Construes it as: speak, and you will obtain all that you wish; once what you want is gained, the mental afflictions will not split you open again. The next verse's 'speech of the sage' is read as Vishvamitra's.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra has Vishvamitra ask Rama to state his heart's craving so it can be settled for good; Rama then shakes off his sorrow like a peacock at the sound of thunder.

practical_reading: The first step out of a heavy silence is often being asked kindly and given room to speak. It also models how to ask someone who has withdrawn: gently, without judgement.
misreadings: Not a promise that every wish will be granted
Not a claim that talking alone cures everything
cautions: Our record has no prasang attached to this verse (prasang is null); link it to the 'Rama comes home and loses interest' story
speaks_to: people who find it hard to ask for help
anyone wanting to support a withdrawn friend or child
not_for: a reader who has tried to speak up and been dismissed, if framed as 'just talk and it goes away'
research_note: Data issue: prasang is null in our record.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.13.8 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 13, titled 'Rejection of Lakshmi', i.e. of wealth). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XIII v. 8.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Good. The commentary reads 'cool and soft to the touch' as standing for kindness and courtesy, 'vātyā' as a mass of wind, and 'paruṣīkṛtāḥ' as made harsh or unbearable. 'Blizzard' is fine; Mitra has 'blasts of wind stiffening frost'.
context: Rama's lament begins with wealth (Lakshmi, fortune). In this chapter he says riches breed vices the way milk feeds a snake's poison, that they soil the learned and brave like dust on gems, and that they bring woe rather than happiness. The next verses list the three rare kinds of men (v. 11).

key_terms.sense: cool and gentle to touch: kind, courteous
toward strangers and one's own people alike
a gust of wind on snow/frost

core_teaching: People are often kind to everyone until money and status harden them, the way cold wind turns soft snow into hard ice.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'cool and soft to touch' as a figure for compassion and courtesy, 'vātyā' as a gathering of winds, and 'made harsh' as made hard to bear.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as people being gentle to friends and strangers until riches harden their hearts, as wind stiffens frost; the surrounding verses say wealth corrupts the learned, the brave and the gentle.

practical_reading: A check on how success or money is changing how we treat people, and a reminder to keep the warmth we had before.
misreadings: Not a claim that all wealthy people are cruel
Not a call to stay poor
cautions: Can feed resentment toward richer relatives or colleagues; frame it as self-examination
speaks_to: someone newly promoted or newly well-off
feeling hurt by a friend who changed after success
not_for: someone in financial hardship who may hear it as consolation-by-contempt for the rich

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.13.11 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 13, 'Rejection of Lakshmi'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XIII v. 11.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Good. 'ajana-nindya' is 'not blamed by people'; 'samadṛṣṭiḥ prabhuḥ' is 'a master/ruler with an even eye'.
context: Still on wealth and fortune, Rama has said riches bring woe and conceal poison like a cultivated aconite plant. Here he names three rare types of person. The verses that follow describe wealth as a deep, rough cave and a great mountain river.

key_terms.sense: a wealthy man no one blames
a hero who does not boast
a powerful person who sees all equally

core_teaching: Wealth, courage and power tend to bring their own vice (blame, boasting, partiality); the person who holds them without that vice is rare.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Raises the objection that some rich people are righteous and famous, and answers with this verse: yes, but such people are rare. He calls the verse self-explanatory.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders the three rarities as a rich man without blemish, a brave man without vanity, and a master without partiality.

practical_reading: Used as a checklist for leaders and achievers: have the money without the arrogance, the courage without the bragging, the authority without favouritism.
misreadings: Not proof that the rich, brave or powerful are bad
Not a male-only standard; the point applies to anyone
speaks_to: parents talking about character with teens
not_for: someone feeling powerless or poor, if used to sneer at others

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.14.10 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 14, on the worthlessness of mere lifespan). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XIV v. 10.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Good. Anandabodhendra reads 'prāpyam' as the highest human goal that must be attained and 'nirvṛti' as the bliss of jivanmukti (liberation while living).
context: After wealth, Rama turns to life itself: the body is like foam on the sea and he takes no pleasure in mere living. In this verse he defines real living. Next he says trees, animals and birds also 'live', but only one who lives by reflection truly lives, and that scripture is a burden to the undiscerning and knowledge a burden to the passionate.

key_terms.sense: what is worth attaining is attained

core_teaching: A life counts as truly lived when it reaches what is really worth reaching, the lasting peace after which grief doesn't return; mere survival is not enough.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'what is to be attained' as the supreme human goal that must necessarily be reached, and 'supreme repose' as the bliss of liberation while living; the next verse's 'mere living' is life without reflection.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders true living as gaining what is worth gaining so that there is no more sorrow; the following verses contrast vegetable and animal life with a life lived by understanding.

practical_reading: A prompt to ask what you are actually living for, beyond getting through the days, and to measure a life by inner peace reached rather than years or possessions.
misreadings: Not a statement that ordinary lives are worthless
Not a reason to despise one's own life when one feels it lacks meaning
cautions: The surrounding verses disparage 'mere living' and the body (foam on the sea); for a reader who feels their life has no value, this framing could deepen hopelessness. Pair with an affirming verse.
speaks_to: feeling that life is only routine
graduates or retirees asking what comes next
not_for: anyone expressing that their life is not worth living
acute grief

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.16.3 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 16, on the faults of the mind). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XVI v. 3.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Good. The commentary defines 'karaṇḍaka' as a vessel woven of bamboo or cane strips; 'wicker basket' is right. The subject is the mind (from v. 1-2, where it roams like a village dog).
context: Rama now describes the mind. Just before this he says it wanders like a hungry village dog; just after, that it is always empty, caught in the net of bad hopes, and roams like a deer that has lost its herd. Later in the chapter he says the mind is harder to master than drinking the ocean (v. 24) and is the cause of everything (v. 25).

key_terms.sense: a woven basket or wicker vessel

core_teaching: The restless mind can't be filled by acquisitions; like a woven basket in water, whatever is poured in runs out, so the emptiness remains.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Defines the 'karaṇḍaka' as a woven bamboo or cane container, and reads the surrounding verses as the mind roaming without discernment, never coming to rest.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the mind seldom finding anything, and even with a good store, being as little content as a wicker vessel filled with water.

practical_reading: If each new purchase, achievement or relationship fades quickly, the problem may be the container, not the contents. Teachers use it to turn attention from getting more to steadying the mind.
misreadings: Not a claim that wanting things is shameful
Not a counsel of despair: Rama names the problem that Vasishtha's teaching later addresses
cautions: Nearby verses are harsh about the mind; quote this one alone
speaks_to: chasing the next goal and feeling empty after each
shopping or scrolling to fill a gap
high achievers who never feel satisfied
not_for: someone in material need, for whom 'riches don't satisfy' can sound glib

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.16.25 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 16, on the faults of the mind). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XVI v. 25.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Mostly accurate, but 'treated with care' should carry the medical sense: Anandabodhendra glosses 'cikitsyam' as 'to be removed like a disease'. 'tasmin sati' is 'when it exists', not quite 'while it is active'. Our line 'Tend to it with care' softens the medical image into nurturing; 'treat it like an illness, with effort (prayatnataḥ)' is closer.
context: At the end of his account of the mind, Rama says subduing it is harder than drinking the ocean or uprooting Mount Meru (v. 24). Here he states its central role, and in the next verse he says hundreds of joys and sorrows spring from the mind like forests from a mountain, but fall away when cut by discernment.

key_terms.sense: the mind is the cause of (all) things/objects
when it exists, the three worlds exist
when it wanes, the world wanes
to be treated (like a disease) with effort

core_teaching: The world we experience depends on the mind, so the mind is the patient: it must be deliberately treated, the way one treats an illness.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'to be treated' as: to be removed, like a disease. The following verse is read as discernment thinning out the mind's hundreds of pleasures and pains.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders the mind as the cause of all exertions and the seat of the three worlds; its weakening weakens worldliness, and it needs careful cure.

practical_reading: When life feels overwhelming, change begins with working on the mind that experiences it, deliberately and consistently, the way one follows a treatment.
misreadings: Not a claim that external problems are imaginary
Not 'it's all in your head' blame
cautions: For a reader with mental illness, 'your world is your mind' can sound like blame; stress that treatment, including professional help, fits the verse's own medical image
speaks_to: feeling that one's outlook colours everything
someone starting a meditation, therapy or self-care routine
not_for: someone facing real external injustice or crisis, if used to dismiss it
research_note: Translation/line nuance flagged (cikitsya = treat as an illness).

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.17.14 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 17, titled 'Breaking of craving', tṛṣṇā-bhaṅga). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XVII v. 14.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Good. The commentary takes 'knotted inside the body' as threaded through the inner mind, matching the bullock's rope threaded through its nose; Mitra renders 'tṛṣṇā' as 'avarice'.
context: After the mind, Rama turns to craving (tṛṣṇā), which he says withers his good qualities the way a mouse gnaws a lute string. Just before this verse, craving pulls people up and down like a bucket in a well; just after, attachment to family spreads its net like a hunter catching birds.

key_terms.sense: a bullock led by a rope

core_teaching: Craving is tied deep inside us and leads us around, the way a nose-rope leads a bullock wherever the driver wants.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'in the body' as threaded through the inner mind, paralleling the nose-rope threaded through a bullock's nose; what the person is made to haul is the load of countless means for gains in this world and the next.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as a man led about like a beast of burden by avarice, which bends his heart as a string bends the beast and is hard to break.

practical_reading: Notice what keeps pulling you: the urge to check, buy, prove or acquire. Seeing the rope is the first step to not being led by it.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all desire or ambition
Not a claim that addiction is simply a moral failing
cautions: For someone struggling with addiction, pair it with practical support; the verse names the pull, it doesn't solve it
speaks_to: feeling driven by wants one doesn't endorse
not_for: someone in early recovery who could hear it as shaming

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.17.43 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 17, 'Breaking of craving'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XVII v. 43.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Acceptable, but 'worry' needs care. Anandabodhendra glosses 'cintā' as dwelling on sense objects (viṣayānusmaraṇa) and cites Gita 2.62, so it means brooding on what one wants, not ordinary anxiety. 'Mantra' (spell, remedy) and 'viṣūcikā' (cholera) are in the original. Our line says 'most sorrow'; the verse says 'all sorrow' (akhilaṁ duḥkham). Our note already explains 'cintā' correctly.
context: Near the end of Rama's chapter on craving, after many images of how craving deceives and wears people down, he says what would release it: dropping 'cintā'. The following verses return to craving's power, grabbing anything like a fish at bait and making even serious people shallow.
core_teaching: Craving is fed by repeatedly dwelling on what we want; stop the dwelling and the sorrow it brings falls away. This is called the cure for the disease of craving.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the verse as the means to give up craving. 'Cintā' here means repeatedly calling sense objects to mind; he cites the Gita's line that dwelling on objects breeds attachment.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as people getting rid of misery by being freed from anxieties, with abandoning cares called the best remedy for avarice.

practical_reading: When a want keeps looping in your head, stop feeding it with attention: change what you look at, rehearse it less, and the grip loosens.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about real problems'
Not 'anxiety is a choice'; it is about rumination on desires
cautions: For someone with an anxiety disorder, 'just give up worry' can feel invalidating; use the sense of letting go of fixation, not suppressing fear
not_for: clinical anxiety, if read as 'just stop worrying'
someone worried about a real danger
research_note: Translation note: 'cintā' = dwelling on desired objects, per the commentary.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.17.50 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 17, 'Breaking of craving'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XVII v. 50.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Good. Anandabodhendra explains the mechanism: craving makes a great person beg, and the humiliation of asking makes him light as grass; he quotes a proverb that a beggar is lighter than cotton, which is lighter than grass. Mitra translates the subject as 'penury'.
context: Rama's chapter on craving piles up images: craving is like a lamp flame that is bright but burns and blackens (v. 49), like a dark Vindhya slope (v. 51). This verse says how quickly it can diminish even the greatest.

key_terms.sense: in the blink of an eye

core_teaching: Craving alone can reduce a wise, brave, steady person to something as light and worthless as grass, in an instant.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: 'Like Meru' means weighty; 'steady' means firm in not grasping. Craving shrinks such a person to grass by reducing him to begging; he quotes a verse that a supplicant is lighter than cotton.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as penury having the power to debase the best of men to straw in a moment, regardless of wisdom, heroism and gravity.

practical_reading: No achievement or status protects us from being made small by wanting; staying grounded in what we value matters more than reputation.
misreadings: Not contempt for people who ask for help or are in need
cautions: The commentary's link to begging could shame people who must ask for help; avoid that angle in a reading
speaks_to: a capable person ashamed of how a want or habit has diminished them
not_for: someone who has had to ask for financial help

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.26.11 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 26, on the impermanence of all that stands against the highest good). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XXVI v. 11.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Good. Anandabodhendra gives two readings of 'truth has turned untrue': what we took as the real self (the body etc.) proves unreal under discernment; or, real knowledge and goodness have become as if unreal. He reads 'the self strikes the self' as the self, identified with the mind, making itself suffer through the mind.
context: Late in his lament Rama surveys a world turned upside down: enjoyments are great diseases and cravings mirages (v. 10). Here he locates the enemy inside: the senses and the mind. Following verses call ego a stain and the intellect weak.

key_terms.sense: the senses themselves are the enemies
the self strikes the self, by itself
by the mind itself, the mind is the foe

core_teaching: Our worst harm comes from within: senses and mind turned against us. The commentary explains this as the self, identified with the mind, causing its own suffering.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: The mind is the enemy because it causes bondage; the self, taking itself to be the mind, in a sense strikes itself by means of the mind, i.e. makes itself suffer.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as our very senses being our enemies before which truth gives way; the surrounding verses list friends as ties, enjoyments as disease, and ambition as a mirage.

practical_reading: Many struggles are inner: self-sabotage, harsh self-talk, habits that undo our own plans. Seeing that clearly is the start of change; Vasishtha later teaches that the same mind can lift itself.
misreadings: Not a reason for self-blame or self-punishment
Not a claim that outside harms don't exist
cautions: 'The self strikes the self' must never be used near self-harm or suicidal thoughts; avoid for readers in crisis
Rama's lament here is bleak; it is the question, not the book's answer
speaks_to: feeling one is one's own obstacle
not_for: anyone with self-harm history or suicidal ideation
someone being harmed by another person

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.26.21 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 26). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XXVI v. 21.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.
translation_note: Fair. Mitra reads 'pātotpāta-paro janaḥ' as people subject to birth and death ('falling and rising'); our 'rising and falling' keeps both readings open.
context: In the same bleak survey Rama says compassion no longer rises and meanness comes easily (v. 20). Here: courage gives way, people rise and fall, bad company is easy and good company hard. Next: all things come and go, and wishes bind us to the world.

key_terms.sense: falling and rising; (Mitra) death and birth

core_teaching: Firmness erodes easily, and bad influences are always at hand while good company is rare, so good company is worth seeking out on purpose.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVI)

good work that the discerning rely on

context: Having finished his lament, Rama turns to questions: how can the mind become clear like a lake (v. 16)? Here: how can one active in the world stay unbound? key_terms.sense: right in the stream of worldly life

core_teaching: Rama's key question: is it possible to be fully active in the world and still not be stained or bound by it, like water on a lotus leaf? The whole teaching answers yes.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as asking how one engaged in worldly affairs can remain untainted, pure and intact like a water drop on a lotus leaf; the next questions ask for an exemplar who crossed the ocean of the world.

commentaries.who: Context in the Sanskrit text (Nirnaya Sagar ed.)

not_for: someone in grief who may hear 'untouched' as 'you shouldn't be affected'

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.31.7 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 31, titled 'Raghava's question'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XXXI v. 7.

key_terms.sense: the wise, those of good understanding
lead it to beauty, make it delightful

core_teaching: Nothing in heaven or earth is so trivial that wise people cannot make it beautiful; Rama is expressing trust that his teachers can transform his bleak view.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'the wise' as minds empowered by austerity and knowledge like the sages present; nothing exists that they could not make delightful. He cites stories where a guru's curse turned into heaven or a death sentence was averted.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as nothing being so trifling on earth or in heaven that the gifted cannot raise it to consequence; the next verse asks how this vapid world can be relished except through ignorance.

practical_reading: A wise eye can find worth and beauty in ordinary, even dull things; seek out those who see that way and learn to see that way yourself.
misreadings: Not 'everything is beautiful if you are positive', dismissing real hardship
cautions: The chapter ends (vv. 21-26) with Rama vowing to give up food, water and finally the body if he gets no answer; never quote that context to a distressed reader
not_for: someone in crisis, given the chapter's ending

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.31.17 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 31, 'Raghava's question'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Vairagya ch. XXXI v. 17.
attribution_note: Rama to the sages, as stated.

context: Rama asks how to escape sorrow and says there is no ending of it without a method (yukti) (v. 16). Here he asks for that method. Then he asks how great people of old reached peace. commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as a request for the best instruction to ward off the world's miseries, either by dealing with affairs or by renouncing them; the chapter closes with Rama's vow to withdraw from all activity if unanswered.

commentaries.gist: Treats vv. 16-17 together without a separate gloss; the following verses are read as Rama asking how the noble-minded of old achieved peace.

practical_reading: The question many people really have: not 'should I quit?' but 'how do I keep doing this without it crushing me?' The book's answer is inner freedom while acting.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of quitting work or family
Not a promise of a quick technique

not_for: someone with suicidal thoughts, if the chapter context is drawn in

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.4.12 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 4, on effort). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra numbers it v. 13 in his Mumukshu ch. IV.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Good. Anandabodhendra stresses 'kramāt' (step by step): it signals doing the work in the proper order, since obstacles arise from departing from it, and a complete action reliably yields its result.
context: Vasishtha opens the long 'effort vs fate' teaching (Mumukshu sargas 4-9). Just before, he defines real effort as action of mind and body along the path taught by the good; anything else is a madman's flailing. After this verse he gives examples of beings who reached the status of Indra or Shiva by effort, and says effort is of two kinds, past and present (v. 17).

key_terms.sense: strives step by step, in due order

core_teaching: Whoever genuinely wants something and works for it steadily and in the right order will reach it, unless they give up halfway.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: 'Step by step' is there to show that setbacks come only from skipping what the right procedure requires; an action carried out completely is bound to bear fruit. The following verses confirm this with examples.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. IV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as one who wishes for riches and perseveres surely gaining them, or else stopping short midway; just before, effort following the counsel of the good succeeds, otherwise it is a madman's antics.

practical_reading: Persistence in the right method matters more than a perfect start. When progress stalls, check the method and keep going rather than quitting midway.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that every goal is reachable by effort alone (Vasishtha himself limits this at 2.6.21)
Not blame for those whose efforts failed through no fault of their own
cautions: Can feel blaming to someone who worked hard and still lost (illness, job loss, infertility); pair with 2.6.21
speaks_to: someone tempted to quit a long project
not_for: someone grieving a loss that effort could not prevent
chronic illness

attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.

core_teaching: There are two kinds of effort: what we did before and what we do now. Present effort can soon overcome the effects of the past.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra's v. 78 describes one who feels a cool calmness within (the rest of his line is lost at a page break), followed by one untroubled by life's long tribulations who does not take the body to be himself.

practical_reading: You don't need to step away from work or family to be calm; aim to be engaged and unhurried inside at the same time.
misreadings: Not detachment as disengagement
research_note: Mitra's text for this verse is partly lost at a page break in the scan.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.14.2 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 14, titled 'Exposition of inquiry', vicāra-nirūpaṇa). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Mumukshu ch. XIV v. 2.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Good. The commentary glosses 'sharpness' as skill in penetrating subtle truth; Mitra translates vicāra as 'reasoning'.
context: Opening the chapter on the second gatekeeper, Vasishtha says one should inquire constantly, with a mind purified by understanding the teachings (v. 1). Here inquiry is medicine. Next: the world is a forest of troubles whose shoots of desire, once cut by the saw of inquiry, don't grow back.

key_terms.sense: the long disease of worldly existence

core_teaching: Sustained inquiry sharpens understanding until it sees the highest truth; it is the great remedy for the chronic illness of worldly suffering.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'sharpness' as skill at plunging into subtle truth; inquiry is what develops that skill.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as understanding sharpened by reasoning coming to see the transcendent state, reasoning being the best medicine for the chronic disease of worldliness.

practical_reading: When stuck in a recurring problem, ask honest questions about it (what is really happening, what do I assume?) instead of only reacting.
misreadings: Not endless overthinking or rumination
Not intellectual cleverness for its own sake
cautions: For ruminating or anxious readers, distinguish inquiry from looping worry
not_for: acute crisis where reflection is not yet possible

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.14.11 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 14, 'Exposition of inquiry'). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Mumukshu ch. XIV v. 11.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Good. Anandabodhendra says 'viveka' here means inquiry, glosses 'do not sink' as 'do not despair', and identifies the gourds as dried bottle-gourds (used as floats).
context: Vasishtha has said that prosperity and liberation are all fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry (v. 10). Here minds opened by inquiry float. Next: those who act with inquiring minds receive the finest fruits, while sorrows are the blossoms of non-inquiry growing in a fool's heart.
core_teaching: Minds opened by inquiry and discernment don't go under in misfortune; like dried gourds in water, they stay afloat.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Viveka here means inquiry; minds that blossom by it do not sink, meaning they do not fall into despair; the gourds are dried bottle-gourds.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as minds of great men expanded by reasoning never being immersed under currents of calamity but floating like gourds on water.

practical_reading: Understanding a hard situation clearly, rather than drowning in it, keeps us afloat while it passes.
misreadings: Not 'thinking people never suffer'
cautions: If someone is sinking, the verse could imply they lack discernment; frame as encouragement, not judgement
not_for: someone in severe depression, if implied that clear thinking alone should keep them afloat

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.14.53 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 14, 'Exposition of inquiry', last verse before the closing stanza). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Mumukshu ch. XIV v. 53.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Good. The commentary reads 'tattva' as the abiding reality of things and the step after it as steadiness of mind.
context: Vasishtha has said that without inquiry nothing true is properly known (v. 52). Here he sets out the chain from inquiry to the end of sorrow. The chapter then closes with a verse urging Rama, endowed with calm, to let clear inquiry shine and make his actions bear fruit.

key_terms.sense: the complete ending of all sorrow

core_teaching: Inquiry leads to knowing what is real; that brings rest in oneself; that rest becomes calm of mind; and calm ends all sorrow.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Tattva is the permanence of the real; knowing it brings steadiness of mind, and from that rest comes calm, which is the end of all sorrow.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as knowledge of truth coming by reasoning, peace of mind by truth, and the tranquillity of mind dispelling human misery; the closing verse urges weighing everything with reason.

practical_reading: Calm can't be forced directly; it follows from seeing a situation truly. Start by asking clear questions.
misreadings: Not a quick fix for sorrow
cautions: 'End of all sorrow' is a spiritual goal; don't promise it to someone suffering now
speaks_to: people interested in reflection or meditation
someone seeking inner peace through understanding
not_for: fresh grief, where 'end of all sorrow' can sound dismissive

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.15.1 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 15, titled 'Exposition of contentment', santoṣa-nirūpaṇa). Located in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937) and in V. L. Mitra's translation (1891); Mitra Mumukshu ch. XV v. 1.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated ('arisūdana', destroyer of foes, is an epithet for Rama).
translation_note: Good. Anandabodhendra says 'the highest good' means liberation, and calling contentment happiness praises the means by naming it after its fruit; 'rest' (viśrāma) is the cessation of the mind's restless distraction.
context: This opens the chapter on the third gatekeeper. Vasishtha goes on: the contented regard a kingdom as straw (v. 2), are never shaken by adversity (v. 3), and find wealth poisonous compared with contentment's nectar.
core_teaching: Contentment is the highest good and is itself happiness; the contented person reaches the deepest rest.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Contentment, as about to be defined, is the highest good, i.e. liberation, and also happiness; it is praised by naming the means after its fruit. 'Rest' is the end of the mind's restless distraction.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as contentment being the chief good and true enjoyment, the contented man getting the best repose; the contented think sovereignty no better than rotten straw.

practical_reading: Notice what is already enough today; contentment is a practice of appreciating what is here, which brings real rest.
misreadings: Not complacency or giving up on goals
Not a reason to accept injustice
cautions: Avoid using it to tell people in hardship to be content with their lot
not_for: someone facing poverty or injustice, if read as 'be satisfied with less'
